Package 1.2: No inline styles or scripts (strict CSP).

The request: Serve the demo's UI under the server's strict Content-Security-Policy without changing how any page looks.

What the package must deliver:
Per-element styles written as data-style and applied by core.js through one constructed stylesheet; the build fails on any inline script, style block, on... handler or style attribute. Done when the build tests pass, including the one that catches an inline style, and every page renders as demo v1.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Find every inline style attribute in the views and in strings built by JavaScript (102 of them).
2. Rewrite each as data-style and teach core.js to turn each distinct value into one rule of a constructed stylesheet, watching for new values with a MutationObserver.
3. Add a global [hidden]{display:none!important} rule.
4. Make build.py refuse inline scripts, style blocks, event-handler attributes and style attributes, and test that.
5. Compare every page with demo v1 at 1440 px.

Decisions:
- data-style plus a constructed stylesheet ([data-style="..."]:not([hidden]){...}) instead of utility classes or setting el.style from script. Why: CSSOM rules are not blocked by the CSP, the page looks the same, and pages that re-render with innerHTML stay CSP-clean without extra code.
- The build refuses inline code rather than relying on a review. Why: One forgotten style= attribute breaks a page silently under the CSP; a build error catches it at once.

Package 10.1: Settings, routers and typed request and response models.

The request: server.py holds most routes as closures and reads the environment in many places. Introduce one settings object read once, split the routes into routers per area that receive their dependencies through FastAPI Depends, and give every route pydantic request and response models, keeping every path, status code and payload as it is.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_rnd/settings.py (pydantic-settings); routers per area; pydantic models for every request and response; the frontend and tests need no changes. Done when server.py only builds the app, the OpenAPI schema describes every route, and a bad request body is a 422 everywhere.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Check which tests depend on exact error text and when the tests set the model key, so reading settings once per app is safe.
2. Write settings.py; read empty variables as unset.
3. Move the routes into routers (core, research runs, projects, intern and lessons; the drafts in draft/api.py; each page in agentic/pages) that take the stores, the gateway and the running jobs through Depends(services).
4. Write request and response models that document and never trim (extra fields allowed, exclude_unset).
5. Reduce server.py to building the app; write test_api_contract (server only builds the app, every route has a model, a bad body is a 422).
6. Run the suite, the gate and the reviewer; fix; commit.

Decisions:
- Response models document and never trim: extra='allow' and exclude_unset. Why: The package promises unchanged payloads; a model that drops or adds keys would silently change what the frontend receives.
- A bad value of a mirrored setting (port, workspace budget) falls back to its default instead of stopping the server. Why: Those values were only read lazily before; failing at import would break make notebook, /mcp and every test over a setting nothing reads at start.
- A JSON body sent without a JSON content type is still read as JSON (uploads excepted). Why: The old routes always parsed the body whatever its type, and curl -d sends a form type; refusing it would change behaviour for existing clients.
- The model tiers and the database URL stay read by models.settings and storage.db. Why: They are read per request (keys, routing) and by command-line tools that build no app; moving them was not needed for the package and is listed as open.

Package 10.2: Accounts, workspaces and roles.

The request: A team of about 1,000 needs to know who acts and to keep each team's work apart. Add sign-in, sessions, workspaces with members and the four roles, enforced on every route; a gate approval records who approved; the company's identity provider (OIDC) is the main sign-in path, with groups mapped to roles.

What the package must deliver:
Password sign-in hashed with argon2, a server-side session in an HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie, the CSRF token kept on writes; every project, draft and session belongs to a workspace; roles enforced in one dependency; OIDC with groups mapped to roles; sessions in the database; one test per write route that the wrong role and the wrong workspace are refused. Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Map the auth scope (an explore agent) and ask the owner the choices the plan left open: when sign-in is required, which role names, who approves a stage's choice, which new screens may be added to the frozen demo.
2. Part A: roles, the accounts store (users, members, sessions, API tokens; only hashes of tokens stored), migration 0012, a request context naming the workspace's Services, a pool of Services per workspace, the guard added by the shared Router to every route from its method and path, password sign-in and the accounts routes, and python -m dclab_rnd.accounts add for the first owner.
3. Test every write route as a member whose role may not and as a member of another workspace using this one's ids; gate, review, fix, commit part A.
4. Part B: OIDC discovery, authorization code with PKCE, a signed ten-minute state cookie, the ID token checked against the provider's keys, groups mapped to roles per workspace; tested against a fake provider.
5. Part C: the sign-in page, the workspace switcher and avatar, Members and API tokens tabs on Admin, the roles table marked enforced, /mcp acting in the token's workspace; checked in the browser with a local test account.
6. Review B and C, fix, gate, commit; then fix the CI failure of the second-workspace test.

Decisions:
- Sign-in only when configured: with DCLAB_AUTH unset the app stays today's single owner on this machine; password or OIDC turns accounts on and needs PostgreSQL. Why: The owner's choice: local development and every existing test keep working unchanged, while a team deployment turns accounts on.
- Show the Admin page's role names (Owner, ML engineer, Reviewer, Business viewer) and store the plan's values (owner, data_scientist, reviewer, viewer). Why: The owner chose the names the product already shows; 'Intern' stays the agent, not a person's role.
- A stage's choice may be approved by ML engineers, reviewers and owners; gates only by reviewers and owners; gate switches, the training opt-in and members only by owners. Why: The owner's choice: the person running a project confirms its stage choices, while sign-offs that guard the holdout need a reviewer.
- The role check is added by the shared Router from each route's method and path, not written per route. Why: A new route cannot be left out by forgetting a decorator; the test of every write route proves the table.

A2 (privacy). The Home agent of every workspace except the server's own was bound to the server's own workspace.
Scenario: As owner of a second workspace, POST /api/drafts returned 201 but the agent never spoke (the error was swallowed in the background task), and POST /api/drafts/{id}/pack raised KeyError, a 500; model use would have been charged to the first workspace's budget and routing.

A3 (behaviour). Jobs of other workspaces never ran under an external worker and were not recovered after a restart.
Scenario: Under make dev (DCLAB_WORKER=external) with password sign-in, a member of a second workspace runs a stage: the job stays queued for ever, because the worker process opened only its own folder's workspace and claims filter by workspace.

B1 (privacy). OIDC sign-in linked accounts on any email claim: an account takeover.

B6 (behaviour). The client secret was sent in HTTP Basic without form-encoding.
Scenario: A secret containing '%', '+' or ':' fails on providers that decode it as RFC 6749 requires.

Scenario: Create a token and click 'Copy and close': the secret stays as hidden text in the modal body until another dialog replaces it.

C2 (behaviour). The token name was escaped twice in the dialog title.
Scenario: A token named 'R&D laptop' showed as 'R&D laptop: copy it now'.

C3 (privacy). The sign-in page showed any text passed in the address as an error.

Package 10.3: Durable jobs and workers.

The request: Background work runs as asyncio tasks inside the server: a restart loses it, leaves projects stuck 'running', and nothing can stop it. Make stage runs, data pipelines, synthetic data and intern sessions rows in a job table run by workers, with progress, cancel, retry and recovery after a restart.

What the package must deliver:
A job table (kind, payload, status, progress, started, finished, error, attempts, cancel requested) and python -m dclab_rnd.worker claiming with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; cancel checked between steps and wired to the Compute page's Stop; a job left running by a dead worker marked interrupted and retryable; a stage stays deterministic. Done when killing the server mid-run and starting it again resumes or cleanly fails the job, and Stop works on the Compute page.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Map every background task the server starts (an explore agent).
2. Write the job store on files (jobs.json under a lock) and PostgreSQL (the job table, migration 0009, one queued or running job per key by a partial unique index).
3. Write the control (checkpoint, progress) and a worker with one dispatcher thread, heartbeats every 5 s and recovery of stale jobs; handlers for the four kinds.
4. Move the draft work out of the route closures, queue jobs from the routes, add checkpoints between stages, pipeline steps, intern tool calls and synthetic design and generation.
5. Add the jobs API (list, read, Stop, Retry) and the buttons on the Compute page; run the worker as its own process under make dev.
6. Check the Done when by hand: kill a real server with SIGKILL mid-run on files and on PostgreSQL, start it again, retry; then two API instances and a separate worker on one database.
7. Gate and reviewer; three review rounds; commit.

Decisions:
- A stop takes effect at the next checkpoint between steps; a stage is never cut. Why: A stage must stay deterministic: same seed, same record. Cutting a stage mid-fit would leave half a record.
- One queued or running job per key, enforced by a unique index. Why: Two app instances must never start the same project's stages; only the database can decide that for both.
- A running job is interrupted only while its heartbeat is still stale, and a worker whose job was taken stops and writes nothing more. Why: Recovery must never take a job from a live worker or let the displaced worker damage the run that took over (findings F1 and R1).
- Job responses leave out the free text a payload carries. Why: An intern message or a prompt for a model is user text; the API strips it as it already strips session messages.

Package 10.5: Live events and locks across several app instances.

The request: With several app instances behind a load balancer, the chat and pipeline streams, the per-draft agent turn lock and the model pause must work when requests land on different instances.

What the package must deliver:
Events as rows with a sequence per draft, the stream woken by LISTEN/NOTIFY and replayed from Last-Event-ID; the per-draft turn lock an advisory lock; the model pause a row with an expiry; tested with two app processes and one worker on one database. Done when a page connected to one instance shows events produced through the other, and two messages to one draft never interleave.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Map what 9.2 already provides on PostgreSQL (numbered event rows, the advisory turn lock, row-locked writes) and what still assumes one process (the stream's poll, the busy check, the model pause in module memory).
2. Check that reply runs inside the turn lock and that the installed psycopg supports waiting for notifications with a timeout.
3. Send pg_notify in the transaction that writes each draft event; one listener thread per server process wakes the streams waiting on that draft; keep the 2-second poll as the fallback.
4. Make 'the agent is still answering' (409) ask the shared turn lock as well as this instance's queued turn.
5. Move the model pause to a model_pause row with an expiry (migration 0011), keyed by endpoint, model and a hash of the API key.
6. Test with two server processes and one worker process on one database; gate and reviewer; fix; commit.

Decisions:
- A notice only wakes a stream; the stream still reads the rows and replays from Last-Event-ID. Why: A missed notice then only delays a stream to its poll, never loses an event.
- The pause key includes a hash of the API key. Why: A new key must not stay paused by the old key's refusal, and the key itself must never be stored.
- A turn's user message and its answer are written under the turn lock. Why: That, not the 409 check, is what guarantees two messages never interleave across instances.

Plan:
1. Run the Home conversation against the local Ollama model (qwen2.5-coder:1.5b) after the OpenAI account refused every request for lack of credit, and see where it stalls.
2. Pull the 'record the answer, mark the question answered, redraw the workflow, ask the next thing' block out of script_turn into one take_answer method, so the script and the model path share it.

The request: Development happens on the developer's machine without containers. Plan:
1. Read the package text, the Makefile's existing targets and the README; check what is installed for watching files (watchfiles is installed but not in the requirements).
2. Write scripts/dev.py with three commands (serve, db-reset, test-db): a reachability check with a start hint, ensure_database (create if missing, drop first on reset, then upgrade), a polling frontend watcher, and uvicorn with reload and one worker.
3. Add make dev, make db-reset (needs CONFIRM=yes) and make test-db; add the README section.
4. Write tests/test_dev_script.py; smoke-test serve by hand on a scratch database (created, migrated, served /api/config, frontend rebuilt on a touched source), then drop it.
5. Run make check-all and the reviewer at the same time; fix the five findings, then the remaining host finding, until the reviewer passes.
6. Record the status row with its open limits and commit.

Decisions:
- The frontend watcher polls file modification times with the standard library. Why: watchfiles is installed but not a declared requirement; polling 36 source files once a second costs nothing and adds no dependency.
- A reset or a create touches only a database named dclab_<letters, digits, _> on this machine; --remote is the explicit override. Why: A reset drops a database with force; a URL left in a shell or in .env could point at a shared server, so the name alone is not a safe guard.
- The authoritative host check asks the server itself (inet_server_addr) before anything is created or dropped, beside the early URL checks. Why: libpq takes the host from many places (the URL, its host and hostaddr query, PGHOST, PGHOSTADDR, a service file); only the server's own address covers all of them in one place.
- make dev reads .env the way the server does. Why: Otherwise the script and the server it starts can silently use different databases.

F1 (behaviour). The frontend watcher thread can die silently, and the frontend is then never rebuilt again.
Scenario: An editor writes and deletes a temporary file next to a source (a vim swap or probe file, a JetBrains safe-write file). changed_since calls is_file() then stat(); the file vanishes in between, stat raises FileNotFoundError outside the try that covers only build(), the thread ends, and make dev keeps serving a stale frontend with one traceback in the terminal.

F2 (behaviour). The safety guard checked only the database's name, not its host.
Scenario: A developer has DCLAB_DATABASE_URL pointing at a dclab_dev database on a staging server exported in the shell and runs make db-reset CONFIRM=yes: the script runs drop database with force on the remote server and ends every session there; make dev would also migrate any remote dclab_* database.

F3 (behaviour). make dev ignored .env, so it and the server could use different databases.
Scenario: .env names a database on another host and the shell does not export it: dev.py falls back to the default local dclab_dev, creates and migrates it and hands it to uvicorn; because the server loads .env without overriding, it uses the local one too. On Linux, where the user's own role often does not exist, make dev fails with 'server did not answer' although .env holds a working URL.

F4 (gap). The README promised more than the code did.
Scenario: The README said 'set DCLAB_DATABASE_URL to use another database; only databases named dclab_* are ever created or dropped', but with a URL to an existing database named myapp make dev exits with 'refusing to create or drop the database myapp'.

F5 (gap). Only the happy path was tested; no failure path was.

The request: Deploy the same image to a cloud: managed PostgreSQL with backups and point-in-time recovery, object storage for tables and artifacts, two or more app instances behind a load balancer with TLS, workers that scale with the job queue, secrets in the cloud's secret manager, logs and metrics in its monitoring; written as infrastructure code with a staging and a production environment. Ask the owner which provider and region before writing anything, and never apply a change to a cloud account without the owner's explicit yes. The owner chose both AWS and Google Cloud and left the region for later.

What the package must deliver:
OpenTofu/Terraform for the chosen clouds, each with staging and production: managed PostgreSQL with PITR, object storage, 2+ app instances behind TLS, queue-scaled workers, a secret manager, cloud logs and metrics. Nothing planned or applied without the owner's yes.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Ask the owner for the provider and region; the answer was both AWS and Google Cloud, region decided later (a variable without a default).
2. Change the app for many instances first: the migration on start under a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a queue-length metric published by each worker, and /healthz and /readyz exempt from the host check for GET and HEAD only (a load balancer probes by IP).
3. Install OpenTofu and write deploy/aws (network, data, ECS app and workers, OpenTelemetry sidecar, autoscaling, alarms) and deploy/gcp (Cloud Run app and worker pool, Cloud SQL, bucket mounted as the workspace, Secret Manager, a declared custom metric for the queue alert), each a module with staging and production.
4. Keep provider downloads out of git and share one plugin cache (764 MB per copy on a nearly full disk).
5. Write tests/test_deploy.py (settings documented, no secret in the code, production keeps its protections, the migration lock) and make deploy-check (fmt and validate for the four environments).
6. Run make check-all and the reviewer; six review rounds, each finding fixed and tested; commit with nothing planned or applied.

Decisions:
- Region is a variable with no default, and no tooling ever runs plan or apply. Why: The owner had not chosen a region, and the package forbids touching a cloud account without the owner's explicit yes.
- On Google Cloud the worker pool is sized by the app itself: one worker holding an advisory lock applies the queue rule through the Cloud Run Admin API. Why: Cloud Run's automatic mode scales on CPU, so a backlog of model-bound jobs (low CPU) would never add a worker; the package requires scaling with the queue.
- On AWS a busy worker holds ECS scale-in protection, and a deployment starts new workers beside the old, which drain and then exit. Why: Stopping a worker mid-job leaves the job interrupted until a person retries it; protection also blocks deployments, so old workers must stop claiming and end on their own.
- Workers run the migration before starting, as the app does, under the same advisory lock. Why: A worker that starts before the app has migrated refuses to run, and after a rollback the old workers would refuse a newer schema, leaving none.
- The first owner is made by a one-off task whose password comes from a secret. Why: A password in a run-task override is recorded in clear text by CloudTrail and returned by DescribeTasks.

Plan:
1. Check the Playwright tooling and install Chromium; have an exploration agent map the exact selectors and actions of each step from the frontend's source, while writing the harness.
2. Write scripts/browser_e2e.py on the pattern of product_e2e (its own server on a temporary workspace, or --base for the container) with four checks: flow, stats, pages and mobile.
3. Add make browser-test, requirements/browser.txt and a CI step in the containers job that keeps screenshots of a failing check.

5. Run make check-all and the reviewer; fix six findings and run on an empty workspace, on files and on PostgreSQL; re-review; fix the last finding; gate and commit.

Decisions:
- Read the numbers the page should show from the API over HTTP, not through the page. Why: Comparing the page with itself proves nothing; the API is the independent source.
- Each page is read when its own load has ended (the 13.1 tracker exported as DC.loading), not after a fixed wait. Why: A location.hash change is a same-document navigation, so 'network idle' returns at once; a fixed sleep is flaky on a slow runner and lets a late error be blamed on the next page or missed.

Package 16.1: The problem-kind interface; today's tasks moved onto it.

The request: DCLab should solve many kinds of machine-learning problems, not only the three tasks it knows. Start with one interface every kind plugs into, and move binary, multiclass, regression and text + tabular onto it without changing behaviour.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_rnd/kinds/ with a typed ProblemKind protocol and a registry (get, detect); the four tasks moved onto it with no change in behaviour; the engine, Solution, prepare_bundle, the runner and Home ask the kind; packs map to kinds (imbalanced -> rare event); Solution gains kind and kind_fields. Done when every existing test passes unchanged, the HyperAck and churn stage records are identical before and after, /api/kinds lists the kinds, and a toy kind runs through all five stages touching only its module.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Count where the code branches on the task (runner 21, engine 17, benchmark 6, service 4, others) and decide which branches belong to a kind.
2. Before touching the engine, record the stage records of eight representative projects (HyperAck, Telco churn, letters multiclass, bike regression, clothing reviews text, the fraud replica with the imbalanced pack, the ticket and delivery replicas), twice, to learn the run-to-run noise.
3. Write the interface as a base class whose every part has a default, so a kind overrides only what differs; auto-register every module that defines KIND.
4. Move the per-task code (target encoding, text handling, machine, metrics and defaults, spec settings, target summary and claim, rare screen, model families) into the five built-in kinds.
5. Route the engine, Solution, prepare_bundle, exports and Home through the kind; add /api/kinds.
6. Re-run the eight projects and compare; write tests including a toy kind through all five stages; run the reviewer; fix; rd-check.

Decisions:
- The runner stays the machine layer keyed by task_type; a kind chooses the machine. Why: The runner's 57 task_type branches compute folds, fits and metrics for four numeric machines; moving them would risk behaviour for no gain until a kind needs a new machine (forecasting, survival), which then adds it in its own package.
- Text + tabular and rare events are kinds that inherit from binary. Why: They run on the binary machines and differ only in detection, defaults, questions and export; inheritance keeps the behaviour identical by construction.
- A pack's defaults (metric, rare-event screen) live in its kind. Why: A pack used to change only labels; through its kind it changes what runs, in one place.
- Parity is measured on stage records with ids and timings normalised, against two baseline runs. Why: Two runs of the unchanged code differed only in project ids, fit timings and one tie between tuning candidates, so any other difference after the change is real.

Package 16.2: The kind acceptance harness and an honest capability matrix.

The request: Each kind is called supported only when it reaches a careful data scientist's decisions on a synthetic replica of a realistic case; the Domain packs page must show that, generated, not hand-written maturity labels.

What the package must deliver:
Each kind ships a replica generator and an acceptance test; make kinds-check runs them all; the Domain packs page and /api/kinds show a capability matrix generated from the results (supported only when the acceptance passes, otherwise partial with what is missing). Done when the matrix is generated, the existing kinds pass, and a failing acceptance turns its row from supported to partial in a test.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Give the interface two hooks: case(seed) (the replica as a person brings it) and accept(run) (the decisions, each checked on the finished stage records).
2. Write a harness that builds the project the way a person would: attach the data and the label file, accept the agent's proposal, write the prediction moment, tick the columns the moment's own words name as written later.
3. Use the existing replicas (fraud, tickets, delivery) and write two new ones in dclab_core: subscription churn (binary) and product reviews (text), each with its traps.
4. Store the results with make kinds-check; build the matrix from the file; label the packs from the matrix and remove the hand-written labels.
5. Test the matrix logic (a failure turns a row partial, a forged 'supported' with a failing check is partial, a never-run kind is partial) and that the committed file matches a fresh run.

Decisions:
- Decisions are checked on the engine's own records (roles of columns, the split description, the metric, the holdout against the stage's baselines), never on a separate computation. Why: The acceptance must judge what DCLab decided, not what a test recomputes.
- Thresholds are principled margins (0.1 above chance or the majority, MAE at most 0.9 times the median's) rather than fitted to the first run. Why: A threshold tuned to the run passes by construction and says nothing.
- The matrix trusts no stored 'supported': it recounts the checks. Why: A result file edited by hand or a partial failure must never show as supported.
- The fraud case runs on the full engine (not quick), in its own test file. Why: Quick mode samples 3000 rows and leaves too few frauds; its own file lets the parallel runner start it first.

input:
Package 17.1: The portable core and its contracts.

The request: Everything DCLab learns to solve must be adoptable by DCLab's main product, not only by this R&D studio; the main product stays in its own repository and is never copied here. Start a pure library with versioned contracts the main product can install and map onto its own planners.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_core/ installable as a wheel; frozen pydantic contracts with a version string (ProblemBrief, DataFindings, SolutionPlan, Decision, Review, SolutionReport); make core-schemas writing their JSON Schemas; an Advisor protocol with a deterministic fallback; boundary tests (no dclab_rnd import, only numpy, pandas, scikit-learn and pydantic, Python 3.10 syntax); a studio adapter project to artefacts and back. Done when the schemas are fresh, the boundary test passes, the round trip loses nothing, and a breaking change fails a test unless its version moves.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Read the main product through gh, read only, to learn its contracts (ProblemSpec, ProblemProfile, MetricPlan, HoldoutPlan, ValidationPlan, ExperimentPlan with governed decision points) and its rules (one training path, train-only statistics, a gateway with a deterministic fallback, compact evidence).
2. Write failing tests first: boundary, contracts, schemas, advisor, adapter.
3. Write contracts.py, evidence.py, advisor.py and schemas.py; give Decision its own version, since a host may store it alone.
4. Add the pyproject, README and make core-schemas; build the wheel and install it in a fresh Python 3.12 environment.
5. Write the studio adapter (dclab_rnd/core_adapter.py).
6. Run the dclab-reviewer; fix all 13 findings before anything depends on v1.

Decisions:
- A pure library at the repository root with its own pyproject, depending only on numpy, pandas, scikit-learn and pydantic, never importing dclab_rnd, never training, calling a provider or touching a database. Why: The main product installs it pinned and must not inherit the studio, a network path or a second pipeline.
- Every output is a frozen, versioned contract readable only with its version, with a frozen baseline per version. Why: Once the main product pins v1, any silent shape change becomes expensive; the version must move with the shape.
- Model help only through an injected Advisor; None means the deterministic path, and the evidence it sees is a summary, never rows. Why: The main product sends every model call through its own gateway with a fallback; the library must work with no model at all.
- Facts carry how they are known: stated with a quote, inferred with a reason, unknown without a value. Why: A host must be able to tell the person's words from the library's guesses.
- The model protocol is called Advisor, not ModelClient, and the pydantic floor is 2.10. Why: It advises and may abstain; and below pydantic 2.10 the generated schemas differ from the published ones.

input:
Package 17.2: Understand the problem: from a description to a problem brief.

The request: Before any data, DCLab must understand the problem or challenge as it is described: the goal and action, what one scored row is, the target or how labels are defined, whether they are complete, the moment, entities, constraints, and the deliverables with their rubric. Home and the intern start from it.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_core.understand: description and file names to a ProblemBrief, every field with its status and quote, open questions ranked by impact, rubric and deliverables, confidentiality words; a model may propose fields, kept only with a quote (Home's rule). Done when four written briefs (fraud challenge, churn, delivery-time regression, ticket routing) give the expected briefs with and without a scripted model, no field is filled without a quote or a stated inference, and the fraud brief lists the API, Docker and report with their points.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Write the four briefs in invented words and the expected brief for each, as tests.
2. Write rules sentence by sentence for each field; the advisor proposes only for fields the rules left unknown.
3. Keep the brief on Home's draft and take from it only what Home's own rules would accept; add the intern's read tool understand_problem and the compact brief in describe_data.
4. Run the reviewer; rewrite the rules to give up rather than guess; add the seven adversarial sentences as negative tests.
5. Run every test that drives Home, then the whole suite on all cores.

Decisions:
- The rules are narrow and give up rather than guess. Why: A wrong moment or target is a leak: an unknown field becomes a question, a wrong stated field silently admits leaky columns.
- A moment is never read inside the outcome's clause, from a bare 'at the moment', or from a 'when' clause whose verb does not start the process. Why: 'Predict whether a purchase is made at checkout' names the outcome, not the moment.
- An advisor's proposal is kept only for an unknown field, with whole quoted words, a quote that supports the value, and a valid value. Why: Home's rule: a model may help, but only with the person's own words behind it.
- Home takes from the brief only a bound target and the action in the user's words; the moment stays with Home's own rules. Why: Home's moment rules were written to refuse exactly the cases the brief's first rules got wrong.
- It lives in dclab_core. Why: The main product should read problems the same way.

Package 17.3: Initial data analysis for decisions, for every task.

The request: Do a first data analysis that leads to decisions for binary, multiclass and regression alike: each finding with its evidence and what it implies for the plan, reading the target only on the training rows.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_core.analyse: tables and a brief to DataFindings, evidence (numbers, never row values) and implication per finding. Common: grain and duplicates, keys and joins across files, entities and target concentration, time and drift, leakage suspects, missingness and whether it predicts the target, types and impossible values. Per task checks. New replicas: ticket routing (multiclass) and delivery time (regression). Done when the findings name each replica's traps with the right implication and hand-checked numbers.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Write the two replicas with their traps: tickets (tiny classes, a label copy resolved_by, duplicated tickets, a late class, a post-moment column) and delivery time (a cap at 60, a heavy tail, a target recomputable from timestamps, a post-delivery rating, negative distances, weather missing in storms, restaurants).
2. Write analyse(): structure on all rows without the target; anything reading the target on the training rows only; every claim measured out of fold against chance.
3. Move all replicas, 15.1's included, into dclab_core/replicas so the main product can run them.
4. Hand-check each replica's numbers in tests; run the reviewer; fix the 14 findings with a failure-path test each and shuffled-label controls.
5. Vectorise the slow paths and time a 200,000-row table.

Decisions:
- Every claim about the target is measured out of fold (two seeded halves) against chance. Why: A column or entity that only memorises rows must not look like signal; shuffled labels must raise nothing.
- A name alone never forbids a column: a post-outcome name without history words is a question, unless the column also predicts the target. Why: Honest columns like previous_rating or delivered_count_last_30d were flagged by name.
- A cap is a spike at the maximum; the tail is read below the cap. Why: A discrete scale is not a cap, and a cap cuts off the tail it hides.
- Ids are compared as text, never through float. Why: Long ids lose digits in a float and two ids collapse into one key.

output:
F1 (leakage). A holdout statistic steered a choice.
Scenario: Training rows 100 to 149 had no conflicting groups and the holdout rows had two; the result reported groups: 2, and that finding bears on the primary metric.

F2 (leakage). An exact copy of a multiclass label went unreported when one class held half the rows or more.
Scenario: Classes at 70/20/10 and a column status_code equal to the label: power 0.294, no finding at all.

F3 (behaviour). Entity concentration fired on random labels.
Scenario: With the fraud labels shuffled, biker_id was still a warning that labels concentrate (64 bikers with positives out of 240); on tickets mean purity was 0.533 under shuffled labels, above the 0.5 cut-off. The test of frauds on bikers proved nothing.

F4 (gap). The delivery replica's heavy tail was not named.
Scenario: On seed 0 the training skew was 0.27, so the finding said 'close to symmetric'; the cap at 60 cut off the tail the replica plants.

F5 (behaviour). analyse() raised on ordinary input.
Scenario: Columns named 'Order Time' and 'Delivered At' gave an id with spaces that the contract refused; a key 'Customer ID' did the same; 600 classes made a statement over 4,000 characters; 40 disagreeing columns exceeded the 30-key limit; a regression with no labelled training rows put NaN in the evidence.

F6 (behaviour). With pandas 3, the main product's version, time columns were never found.
Scenario: With future.infer_string on, text columns have the str dtype; the time detector returned nothing, so no drift and no recompute leak were found.

F7 (behaviour). The name rule flagged honest history columns as leaks.
Scenario: previous_rating, response_time_sla_target, delivered_count_last_30d, avg_rating, last_order_completed and prior_outcome all became warnings to keep out.

F8 (behaviour). Decimal coordinates were called identifiers to keep out.
Scenario: On the fraud replica the identifier list held the pick-up and drop-off latitudes and longitudes, which carry the planted signal; a plan following it would drop them.

F9 (behaviour). Labels coded 1 and 2 were misread.
Scenario: With 2 meaning fraud at 0.5%, class 1 was taken as positive and the positive rate reported as 99.5%, so the rare-event regime was missed.

F10 (behaviour). Long ids lost digits in the label join.
Scenario: Two different 18-digit ids became the same number through float, inflating rows marked; 20-digit ids wrapped to negative.

F11 (gap). Multiclass missingness was never compared with the target.
Scenario: Only regression and binary checked whether missingness predicts the target, though the package asks it for every task.

F12 (behaviour). The cap check fired on discrete targets.
Scenario: A uniform integer target from 0 to 39 was reported capped at 39 with 2.5% at the cap.

F13 (gap). Multiclass analysis was slow on large tables.
Scenario: At 200,000 rows by 50 columns, multiclass took 30 s, about 26 s of it in group-by lambdas computing modes.

F14 (gap). Binary drift missed positives that appear only later.
Scenario: A positive rate of 0 in the first third and above 0 later was never flagged, because the check needed a positive early rate.

Package 17.4: The solution plan: decisions with reasons and alternatives.

The request: Turn the brief and the findings into a plan a careful data scientist would write: one decision per point, each with the findings it rests on and the alternatives set aside; the studio proposes it and a person can override a decision with a reason, as a recorded move.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Write plan() with one decision per key and validate(), which refuses a plan that ignores a critical finding.
2. Add the compact plan to Solution.propose(), read on a seeded 80% of rows, and the adapter solution_fields_from_plan.
3. Test the replicas' decisions; run the suites that use propose().
4. Run the reviewer; for adoption, reuse the studio's governed set_solution move instead of a parallel path: the intern's adopt_plan tool.
5. Fix the 11 findings with 12 new tests; add adopt_plan's refusal case; re-run the judgment suite for the new project tools; rd-check.

Decisions:
- Only a person's override sets a finding aside; a model's override is checked like any proposal. Why: Otherwise a model can mark a decision 'overridden' and skip the leakage checks.
- The grouping entity is the one the person names, else the one that tells the target out of fold, with at least 10 values. Why: Without a brief the first entity by column order was account_id with 3 values, which makes grouped folds degenerate.
- A plan is adopted through the existing set_solution move (graph check, log, memory, audit). Why: The main product's rule, and this repository's: no parallel system for an existing concern.
- propose() adds the plan beside its own fields and leaves them unchanged. Why: Many callers read the proposal; the plan is advice until it is adopted.

input:
Package 17.6: Review and improve: error analysis and the next experiments.

The request: Do not stop at the model screen: look at where the first model fails on the training rows, form hypotheses that cite the measured weakness, and try the change they point to on the same folds, with the holdout untouched until the end.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_core.review: error analysis by segment, class, range and entity; hypotheses citing measured weaknesses; experiments ranked by expected gain and cost; at most N recorded rounds on training folds; holdout once. Done when on the fraud replica a round finds the behaviour features or on the regression replica the cap, the improvement is measured on folds, and the holdout is used once.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Add runner support for experiments learned on the fit fold only: a log target, a median loss, predictions held to the fit rows' range, balanced class weights.
2. Write review.py: weaknesses from the leader's out-of-fold errors, hypotheses that must cite them, experiments ranked runnable first.
3. Run at most 2 rounds in the models stage on the same folds; keep a change only by the rule; the final stage trains with what was kept.
4. Try it on the delivery replica at its usual size (at 1,500 rows the gain was within noise and rightly not kept).
5. Run the reviewer; fix the 7 findings without adding scipy to the core (a small t-table).

Decisions:
- A change is kept only if its paired gain beats the tuning margin (relative when the engine's is) and the one-sided 90% t bound (1.89 standard errors with 3 folds). Why: Mean above one standard error keeps a change with no effect about 21% of the time per round.
- A change the leader cannot make is tried on the best family that can, kept only if it beats both the leader and that family's own screen. Why: Otherwise the gain of switching family is credited to the change.
- Hypotheses must cite a measured weakness; check refuses one that cites nothing measured. Why: A model may propose hypotheses later (18.6); code decides whether they rest on evidence.
- At most two rounds, on the same folds, holdout once. Why: More rounds on the same folds make the training-CV score more optimistic; the claim says it is.

Package 17.7: The solution report, from the records.

The request: Write the solution report a person or the main product can read: the problem, what the data shows, the decisions and why, results with intervals, limits and next steps, with every number taken from a record and no claim of production readiness.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_core.report: a SolutionReport and its rendering (Markdown, HTML, PDF) with the problem, findings, decisions, results with intervals, limits, next steps and a deliverables map when a rubric exists; every number from a record; the prose through the citation check. Done when each replica project's report renders, every number is traced to a record by a test, and no sentence calls a model production-ready.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Built in an isolated worktree by a sub-agent: build() writes the report from the brief, findings, plan and stage records; numbers enter only through record paths.
2. Render Markdown and HTML purely; import reportlab only inside to_pdf (an optional extra), so the core keeps its four dependencies.
3. Write the studio adapter and trace every number of the three replica reports in tests.
4. Two dclab-reviewer passes; fix all 11 distinct findings with tests; merge into main.

Decisions:
- The prose is written by code, never a model; a line is kept only when every number in it traces to a record path. Why: A report for a reader or a grader must not invent or round away a number.
- The core has its own citation check rather than importing dclab_rnd/cited.py, with the same readiness rules. Why: The core may not import the studio.
- Odd record shapes cost a line, never the report, and a section that fails is named in the limits. Why: A report that crashes on a broken record says nothing; one that says what is missing is useful.
- The PDF is an optional extra imported only inside its function. Why: reportlab is not one of the core's four dependencies.

input:
Package 18.2: The problem analyst, measured.

The request: Measure the problem analyst (a model that reads a person's description and column names and proposes the brief fields the rules left open) against the rules alone before anyone relies on it, with the gate written before the run and the sealed set run once, under a euro cap the owner sets.

What the package must deliver:
The analyst's prompt and wiring into understand; 24 written briefs of every kind (dev 12, sealed 12) with the expected fields; a measurement of right and wrong fields with the rules alone, with the analyst, and with a plain prompted model. Done when, with the analyst, more fields are right and none is wrong that the rules left unknown, measured on the sealed set once, with its cost.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Declare the problem_analyst purpose (it sees the description and file and column names, never values) and add its data-limit test, which sends a real request through a capture gateway.
2. Write dclab_rnd/core_advisor.py: the gateway Advisor, one capped client per purpose, the pinned prompt as the system message and the evidence as JSON.
3. Write 24 briefs of every kind with their expected fields, dev 12 and sealed 12, the sealed file fingerprinted; include traps (no target column, no moment, a brief that has chosen no target, near-empty briefs).
4. Build the harness with three readers (rules alone, rules with the analyst, a plain prompted model), score eight fields as right, wrong, missed or abstained, and fix analyst_gate_v1 in code before any run.
5. Ask the owner for a yes and a cap (granted: EUR 0.10). Run dev first while the reviewer reads the harness; hold the sealed run until the review's fixes are in.
6. Fix the nine review findings; tune the scorer and the prompt's definition of the horizon on dev only; re-run dev twice; then run the sealed set once.
7. Record the result in the playbook and the campaign folder, run rd-check, commit.
8. Follow-up for the errors the analyst cannot touch: the brief checker, with its own gate fixed before its one run.

Decisions:
- The analyst is offered only the fields the rules left unknown, and a value is kept only when whole quoted words of the description support it. Why: A wrong moment or target is a leak; the rules give up rather than guess, so a model should only fill what they left open, with the person's own words as evidence.
- analyst_gate_v1 has three checks on the sealed set: more fields right than the rules alone, no wrong field among those the rules left unknown, and no field the rules read changed. Why: Part 7: a role is on only when it beats the deterministic path with no more unsafe moves.
- A plain prompted model is a third reader, scored the same way. Why: It shows what the quote check and the rules add over taking a model's answer as it comes.
- Dev runs first; the sealed set waits for the review's harness fixes. Why: The sealed set runs once; a harness bug found after it would waste it.
- A run with any failed request is stored as _unscored, prints no scores and does not use up the sealed set. Why: One timeout or a cap reached mid-run must not make the package's Done when impossible to meet.
- One sealed gold was made stricter before its run: in s06, 'before the next review' is the end of the outcome window, not the prediction moment. Why: The reviewer showed the gold would accept that wrong value in the analyst's favour; fixing it before the run keeps the run honest, and the change is recorded.
- Follow-up: the brief checker turns a reading that disagrees with a rule-read field into an open question with both options, and never changes the field. Why: All four remaining analyst errors were the rules' own values, which the analyst is never offered; a silent model override would be an unsafe move.
- The brief checker was left off and not tuned after it failed by 0.3 points. Why: Its gate was fixed before the run; a stricter unit rule or prompt needs a new measurement on new briefs.

output:
R1 (behaviour). A reply cut short by the token limit counted as the model declining to answer, so a broken run would be scored and use up the sealed set.
Scenario: gpt-6-luna reasons by default and the 700-token limit includes the reasoning. A fake client returning empty content with finish_reason 'length' on 3 dev briefs gave 6 requests, no failure recorded, and verdict fail. On the sealed set this writes a real fail and the set can never run again. Prose without JSON, or two JSON objects in one reply, did the same.

R2 (behaviour). Correct prediction moments were scored wrong, so a correct analyst would fail the gate.
Scenario: Scripted dev answers 'as soon as it is submitted, before any response or resolution' (d03) and 'when the cart page loads, before checkout' (d09) were scored wrong and counted as new errors; the same wording would hit six sealed briefs.

R3 (behaviour). Any failed request used up the sealed set for good.
Scenario: One transient 429 or a workspace cap reached mid-run still wrote ANA-NNN_sealed.json with every value and score; sealed_runs() then refused any further sealed run, and results may not be deleted. With --cap-eur 0 every request was refused and the set was used up the same way.

R4 (gap). Some expected answers were too lenient and accepted wrong values.
Scenario: Sealed s06's moment gold accepted 'before the next review', the end of the outcome window, in the analyst's favour. On dev, 'on the first day of each month' passed as a horizon, 'weekly, on Mondays' too, and short words had to match exactly, so 'sees' failed 'see'.

R5 (gap). The plain model was penalised for formatting.
Scenario: A plain answer 'Binary' or a target in backticks counted as wrong, while the analyst arm dropped invalid values as missed, so the plain arm's wrong count mixed formatting with judgement.

R6 (gap). The CLI's refusals and a real cap refusal had no test, and one assertion stopped testing anything once the rules improved.
Scenario: No test covered refusing with no model, an unpriced model, no --cap-eur, or an estimate above the cap; the new_wrong assertion sat under an if.

R7 (privacy). Calling the CLI's main() from a test loaded .env into the test process.
Scenario: test_analyst_measure called main(), which loaded the owner's real key and model into os.environ for the rest of a serial test run, where any later test could send a paid request.

R8 (gap). The plain arm skipped the evidence check.
Scenario: It called advisor.ask directly, so the no-rows check that guards every role was never run on its evidence.

R9 (gap). The rules' sealed scores were printed before the sealed run.
Scenario: Plan mode on the sealed split printed the rules-alone numbers, which invites tuning the rules on the sealed set.

R10 (behaviour). The brief checker's CLI priced and routed itself as the problem analyst.
Scenario: Tier, model, local flag and price came from route('problem_analyst') and the analyst's prompt length; if the analyst were routed to a local tier while the checker served a priced one, the cap refusal was skipped and the checker ran with no cap. The estimate also left out the rules' readings it is sent.

R11 (latent). The checker could raise two disputes on one field, and the measurement kept whichever came last.
Scenario: A model returning task as multiclass and as regression gave the person two questions with two options each; proposal_right depended on the answer's order.

input:
Package 18.3: The data investigator, measured.

The request: Build the data investigator, a model role that reads the column names and kinds against the prediction moment (never values) and proposes columns written after the outcome and entities whose rows repeat, and measure it against the rules alone on planted traps before it is used.

What the package must deliver:
A role that reads DataFindings and the column names and kinds, never values, and proposes when each column is written relative to the moment, suspected leaks, entities and meanings; each proposal becomes a check that analyse or the leakage audit runs. Measured on the replicas and the benchmark: planted traps found and clean columns falsely accused, with and without the role. Done when it finds more planted traps than the rules alone without raising false alarms above the gate.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Read the Role API of 18.1 and the analyse checks it would advise (_leakage, _entities).
2. Write DATA_INVESTIGATOR in dclab_core/analyse.py: evidence is the column names, kinds, missing and distinct shares, the moment, the target name and the row count; the answer proposes suspects and entities.
3. Make each proposal a test that code runs exactly as a telling name is tested, in its own slots, so it can add suspicion and never clear a finding.
4. On benchmark v2's dev split, see which traps the rules miss and add two general rule checks: a value missing exactly with the outcome (missing-indicator power) and two columns that add up to the target (both kept out by the plan).
5. Build the harness: dev split plus two replicas for building, the sealed test split for one run; three readers (rules, rules with the investigator, a plain model on names alone); traps found and clean columns accused; investigator_gate_v1 fixed before any run.
6. Add the data_investigator purpose and its data-limit test; run the reviewer; fix its findings; rd-check; commit; ask the owner for a cap.
7. Run dev, then the sealed split once (owner's cap EUR 0.30); record; commit.
8. Follow-up (Step 1): the sealed run's false alarms all came from strong honest columns on a real table; change the rules so such columns become questions, review it, and record that the sealed split is no longer blind for the rules.

Decisions:
- The investigator sees names, kinds and shares, never a value. Why: Column names and timing carry most of the leakage meaning; values would need a data-limit exception, and the purpose's test proves none is sent.
- A proposal never becomes a finding by itself: it is tested by code the way a telling name is, in its own slots. Why: A model can add suspicion but must never clear a rule's finding or push one out; code decides on measured power.
- investigator_gate_v1: on the sealed split, more planted traps found than the rules alone, and no more clean columns accused. Why: Finding more traps is worth nothing if it costs false alarms that make a person ignore the warnings.
- Improve the rules first on dev, then measure the investigator on top of them. Why: The role is judged on what the rules cannot do; a weak baseline would flatter it.
- Evidence is one compact summary line per column, not a list of records. Why: The evidence guard reads a list of same-shaped records as a table and refuses it; a line per column is honest summary data and passes the guard.
- After the sealed run, the strong-column rule was designed from the wine false alarms, and this is recorded in the campaign manifest. Why: Any later rules-alone number on that sealed split is no longer blind; benchmark v3 will be the next blind set.

R1 (leakage). A sum-identity finding never reached the plan and made the rules' own plan invalid.
Scenario: On a table where morning + afternoon = target, core_plan gave features.forbidden [] and validate reported 'F-leak-sum-morning-afternoon is critical but None is not in features.forbidden'. The intern's adopt_plan then refused every regression project with such a pair, while the harness counted the trap as found.

R2 (leakage). An investigator answer could remove a rule's entity warning.
Scenario: Columns c0..c5 with 5 values each, then customer_id sharing the label: the rules alone warned on customer_id; after the investigator proposed c0..c5 as entities, six info findings appeared and the customer_id warning was gone, because proposals joined the same candidate list, cut to 6.

R3 (behaviour). The sum identity accused a clean column.
Scenario: final_amount equal to the target plus discount, 70% zeros: the median test said they add up to the target, giving a critical F-leak-sum on the clean discount column. Real tables (a final fare beside a mostly-zero tip) would hit it.

R4 (gap). The gate's false-alarm count missed entity false alarms.
Scenario: A scripted investigator naming every column an entity gave 12 clean dev columns an entity warning (on_promotion, months_active, prior_claims); the gate counted none, though plan._split would group folds by months_active and validate would refuse a stratified split.

R5 (gap). Wide tables were cut without saying so.
Scenario: A 221-column table sent 150 column lines and no total, so the model could not know columns were missing.

R6 (gap). The sum identity was slow on large tables.
Scenario: 780 column pairs converted to float inside the loop: 17.7 s at 1M rows by 40 columns, 8.3 s of analyse's 20.7 s at 500k rows, on every regression table in core_plan.

R7 (gap). The delivery differed from the package text without saying so.
Scenario: The playbook asks for the replicas and benchmark v3; the harness used benchmark v2 with the two replicas in dev only, and per-column meanings, 'when written' and a leakage-audit hook were not built.

R8 (leakage). Follow-up rule: two real leaks in one table became questions instead of leaks.
Scenario: Two planted leaks (y plus noise, 3y plus noise) each had power about 0.9999 but a Spearman of only about 0.75 with each other, so both counted as 'unrelated strong columns' and became info questions; a leak beside an honest driver of power 0.97, and a leak with its own noisy copy, did the same. The plan forbade nothing and told the person 'the task may simply be easy'.

R9 (leakage). Follow-up rule: validate did not protect columns held for confirmation, so a model could release them.
Scenario: The intern's adopt_plan with an advisor override features.to_confirm = [] passed validate and set the solution with nothing forbidden; before the rule these columns were critical and the change was refused.

R10 (gap). Follow-up rule: the plan's reason text was wrong when columns were held for confirmation.
Scenario: With an empty forbidden list it said 'No column looks written after the moment by name, power or recomputation' while to_confirm held columns of power about 0.9999.

R11 (gap). Follow-up rule: the rule's cost was not measurable on dev, and planted leaks turned into questions were not counted as misses.
Scenario: No dev case put a planted leak beside a strong honest column; the scorer ignored info findings, so a leak demoted to a question was invisible.

R12 (gap). Follow-up rule: column power was computed twice.
Scenario: On 200k rows by 80 columns, _leakage went from 8.1 s to 13.7 s (binary) and 8.3 s to 18.5 s (multiclass).

Plan:
1. Write connectors/db.py: connections named DCLAB_DB_<NAME> holding a SQLAlchemy URL; allow a table pick or one read-only SELECT, row-capped.
2. Check the query under two SQL dialects and wrap it with a row limit; refuse anything that writes.

Package 9.2: The database schema and migrations.

The request: PostgreSQL only, for a team of about 1,000 users, runnable locally and later in the cloud. Build the schema and migrations and a PostgreSQL implementation of the 9.1 storage interfaces, tested against a real database, never a mock.

What the package must deliver:
SQLAlchemy 2 models and Alembic migrations; documents read whole as JSON columns, what lists filter or sort on as indexed columns; append-only logs with a sequence per parent; immutable stage records; DCLAB_DATABASE_URL switches the product; a pooled connection; no raw SQL from request input. Done when the whole suite and make product-e2e pass against PostgreSQL and the projects list stays fast with 10,000 projects (measured, with the query plan).

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Ask the owner before touching the local PostgreSQL server: create two new databases (dclab_dev for working data, dclab_test for the tests, which empty it) and install the psycopg driver.
2. Write the schema: ten tables (workspace, app_user, membership, project, stage_record, activity, transition, draft, draft_event, intern_session) and the first migration; python -m dclab_rnd.storage upgrade.
3. Share the 'new document' builders between the file and PostgreSQL stores so both create identical documents.
4. Write the PostgreSQL stores: row locks for update, draft event numbers from an UPDATE of the draft row, the agent turn as an advisory lock, every query filtered by workspace.
5. Write one contract test that runs the same behaviours against both backends.
6. Switch the server with DCLAB_DATABASE_URL; run the whole suite on PostgreSQL and on files, and make product-e2e on PostgreSQL.
7. Measure a page of 50 projects among 10,000 with timings and the query plan; add a test that the migration and the models describe the same database; add make test-pg.

Decisions:
- Two fixed databases on the developer's machine: dclab_dev and dclab_test. Why: The tests empty their database; sharing one with working data would delete the owner's projects on every test run. A temporary database per run needs create and drop rights and can leave strays after a crash. The owner asked why two and agreed.
- A document read whole is JSONB; what a list filters or sorts on is a column with an index. Why: Stage records, solutions and drafts are always read whole, while lists need indexed workspace, status and time columns to stay fast at thousands of projects.
- Keep the file stores and switch with one setting. Why: Both backends stay tested by the same suite and contract test, and a laptop without PostgreSQL still runs.
- Each workspace folder is one workspace until accounts exist. Why: Accounts come in 10.2; until then the folder is the only identity a request has, and isolation can already be tested per workspace.

The request: Add money to the gateway: price each request from one dated table, enforce per-run, per-project and per-workspace caps before a request is sent, and show real spend on the Compute and Admin pages. Never guess a price.

What the package must deliver:
One price table (euros per million tokens, with a date); caps per project per run, per project per month and per workspace per month; the wizard's euro budget becomes a real cap; a refusal says how much is left; spend from the usage table on Compute and Admin; 'not metered' removed only where it is now true; an unknown model is 'price not configured' and counted in tokens only. Done when a scripted run over its cap is refused before the request is sent and the pages show euros from the usage table.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Write dclab_rnd/models/prices.py (or DCLAB_PRICES_FILE) with a date per table; a model without a price is counted in tokens only; a request to a model on this machine is free.
2. Add the cost to the usage log (migration 0003) and the caps to the gateway: the intern session's max_eur (run), the wizard's budget (project, per month), DCLAB_WORKSPACE_MONTHLY_EUR (workspace).
3. Show the euros on Compute and Admin, and how many requests have no price.
4. Update the test that asserted spend is not tracked, since that is exactly what changed.
5. Run check-all and the review; fix the six findings with tests; render the two pages; commit.

Decisions:
- Refuse a request when its upper-bound cost could pass a cap, checked and reserved under a lock. Why: Checking 'already over' lets the request that crosses the cap through, and an unlocked check lets concurrent requests near the cap all pass.
- The upper bound is the prompt's characters divided by three times the input price plus max_tokens times the output price. Why: The real token count is known only after the reply; an estimate that is never lower than the truth keeps the cap a cap.
- Never guess a price; an unpriced model is counted in tokens. Why: A guessed price would make a cap look enforced while it is not; showing 'no price' tells the owner what to configure.

Package A2.2: The validator in front of every agent write.

The request: Make the workflow validator impossible to skip: every write tool declares the move it makes, the runtime asks studio.graph.check as the agent before the handler runs, and a refusal is logged and returned to the model with the reason and the rules. The Home agent's draft writes get their own checks.

What the package must deliver:
Each write tool declares its move (run_stage, set_solution, approve_gate, approve_stage, capture); a refusal is logged by graph.log and returned as the tool result with the reason and cited rules; a test enumerates the registry and fails if a write tool has no move; Home writes (record, set_pack, propose_workflow, simulate_data) get workflow validation, a pack list and one simulation at a time. Done when a test calls every write tool with a move the validator refuses and gets the reason and a logged transition, and no write tool bypasses the check.

output:
Plan:
1. Read the validator (studio/graph.py) and list which project writes it checks; four (create_project, attach_data, set_settings, propose_solution) were never checked or logged.
2. Write the test first, as a new file while A2.1 was under review: refuse every project write tool and fail when a new write tool has no refusal case.
3. Make registration refuse a write tool without a move, and send every write through its scope's guard: the project guard asks graph.check as the agent; the draft guard checks the pack list and the user's choice, workflow.validate and one preparation at a time.
4. Add graph checks for the four uncovered writes (for example the agent may not replace the data under a solution the owner signed).
5. Run check-all and the review; fix the two findings; commit.

Decisions:
- The guard lives in the registry's call path, not in each handler. Why: A handler that checks the graph itself can be written without the check; a registry that refuses to run a write without a guard cannot be bypassed by a new tool.
- A refused Home workflow keeps the current workflow instead of falling back to the template. Why: Falling back silently replaced work the person had already seen with a generic template.
- The create_project transition logs the name but not the user's goal. Why: The goal is the user's free text and the transition log is the future training source (A6.1); the reviewer noted it would carry up to 300 characters of the task.

The request: Build the judgment suite the Benchmark page describes: at least 20 seeded cases, each a small table with a planted trap, its prediction moment and the expected behaviour; score leak caught, false alarm, unsafe move refused and citations that exist; run the standard plan and a deliberately bad policy in make rd-check and expect the bad one to fail the right cases.

dclab_rnd/agent_eval/ with at least 20 cases; traps: a post-outcome column, a noisy copy of the target, an identifier that predicts the target, a time column with a random split, group leakage, duplicated rows across the split, a unit conversion of the target, a constant column, informative missingness that is not a leak. Done when the standard plan scores on every case and a broken policy that ignores the audit fails the cases it should.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Map the building blocks: the intern's tools, the validator, the column audit, the engine's records.
2. Write the suite: seeded cases in cases.py (each a 1,500-row table), three scripted policies (the intern's standard plan, the audit's own defaults as a reference, a deliberately bad policy that ignores the audit and tries two moves out of order), scoring in run.py from what each policy left behind in a fresh project, and a runner that stores an AEV result that is never overwritten.
3. Put the scores on the Benchmark page's leaderboard; check it in the real page.
4. Write the tests: the whole suite runs once in the test gate, the bad policy fails what it should, the scorecard is pinned.
5. Run check-all and the review; fix seven findings, which changed the scores; update the pinned scorecard and the status row; re-check; fix the last wording; commit.

Decisions:
- Code scores what the policy left behind, as the engine reads the solution: a leak counts as caught only if the engine keeps it out of the features. Why: A policy that names a leak in a role the engine still models has not kept it out; scoring the declaration instead of the engine's behaviour gave a false catch.
- Case column names avoid the R&D's precedent names. Why: A name the standard plan already knows would measure a lucky name match, not the policy's judgment.
- The repeated-rows case is an engine check, the same for every policy, kept outside the policy scores. Why: The note comes from the data stage whatever the policy does; counting it gave the bad policy a catch it did not make.
- Each case has its own prediction moment, given to every policy. Why: Whether a column is a leak depends on the moment; a single customer-snapshot moment made the patient and regression cases unanswerable.
- What the standard plan should forbid on unseen tables is left to the owner. Why: The choice is between today's 1 of 13 leaks with 1 false alarm and the audit's 10 of 13 with 3 false alarms in 20: a trade-off for the person who carries the risk.

1. Write studio/memory.py: a note is one line built from column names, the task, the metric, the prediction moment, stage and option ids and the reason, never from the table.
2. Hook notes into the moves that decide (a solution saved by the intern or a person, a stage approved, a gate approved); a person changing what the agent or the rule decided becomes a correction that says what changed.

The request: Write the recipe for corpus v4: the 330 declarative examples of v3 plus trajectory examples, split by whole project (about one in five held out), with v3's quality gates (no benchmark contamination, no near-duplicate prompts across the split). Generate nothing until at least 50 trajectories from at least 10 projects exist; until then print how many exist. Keep generated files out of version control as for out_v3.

What the package must deliver:
A corpus v4 recipe mixing v3's declarative examples with trajectories, held out by whole projects, with the number of held-out projects shown against the threshold. Done when the Policy model page shows 'N of 50 trajectories' from the real count and stage 2 is marked ready only at the threshold.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Define a trajectory: one opted-in project's move log or one agent run on it, with at least 3 decisions.
2. Write studio/corpus_v4.py: next_move examples (state, the moves or tools on offer, the last three decisions -> the move made; only allowed moves and working steps) and judge_move examples (a proposed move -> the validator's verdict, failed checks and cited rules); the split by project; v3's gates; make sft-v4 writes nothing below the threshold.
3. Show the real count on the Policy model page and mark stage 2 ready only at both thresholds.
4. Run the review; it simulated 12 standard-plan projects on the Telco sample and found the gates did not work on realistic data; fix eight findings with a realistic fixture; fix the re-check's one; commit.

Decisions:
- Mask the project's own ids (<project>, <run>) in prompts and targets, and count only distinct trajectories toward the threshold. Why: Two projects that decide the same must make the same example; otherwise twenty identical standard-plan runs look like twenty trajectories and pass the duplicate gate.
- A project is in validation when its own id hashes there (about one in five), so it never changes split as the workspace grows; a fallback, when none hashes there, is named in the manifest. Why: Taking the first fifth by hash rank moves projects between splits when new ones arrive, so a later build would train on an earlier build's validation.

The request: Add shadow mode to the gateway: a purpose can name a shadow model that receives the same request; its answer is stored and compared (same tool chosen? same validated output?) but never used. Show agreement rates on the Admin page. Switching a purpose to the tuned model requires a reviewer's approval, recorded in the audit trail, and can be undone in one setting.

The tuned model as an optional tier, with a shadow mode that runs it beside the current model and logs disagreements without acting on them. Done when shadow mode logs disagreements for a week of scripted traffic and the validator still sees only the production model's moves.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Map the gateway: tiers, purposes, Bound, usage, the intern's long-lived client.
2. Write models/routing.py (a purpose's serving tier, its shadow, the history; file or table, migration 0007) and models/shadow.py (compare the first tool call and its arguments, log without prompt, arguments or answer).
3. In the gateway, copy the caller's messages first, answer from the served model, then send the copy to the shadow in a background thread; never return it, never count it in usage or budgets; only a local tier may shadow.
4. Add the tuned tier, read only from DCLAB_TIER_TUNED_*, never falling back to another model; POST /api/models/routing with a reviewer and a reason; the Admin page's purpose table with serving tier, shadow and agreement.
5. Test a week of scripted traffic and an intern run whose shadow proposes moves; rerun the judgment suite (AEV-008); review; fix five findings and one more from the re-check; commit.

Decisions:
- Only a local tier can shadow. Why: A shadow copies every request; locally it costs nothing and no cap needs to see it, and no data goes to another provider.
- The shadow's reply is never returned, never shown to the validator and never counted in usage or budgets. Why: A candidate model must prove itself beside the current one before it decides anything.
- An approval is for one model at one endpoint; a different model under the same tier name serves nothing until approved. Why: An approval tied to the tier name lets any later model inherit a reviewer's yes it never earned.
- Moving a purpose back to its own tier is one setting, for anyone. Why: Undoing a risky switch must be easier than making it.
- Agreement compares the first tool call and its arguments only. Why: It is what can be compared deterministically now; whether the shadow's move would pass the validator ('same validated output') is written as open.

Package PRE-dclab-notebook: The first DCLab notebook: projects, the prediction contract and the five-stage engine on the person's own data.

The request: Remove what does not serve the goal from the data and the UI, then redesign the R&D frontend as a product: a data scientist or ML engineer comes in, creates a project and builds a model of any kind, in any industry, the agentic way instead of writing the pipeline by hand, a more agentic Colab.

What the package must deliver:
First trim the Studio UI to what serves the research goal. Then add dclab_rnd/studio/: projects on disk, any CSV, TSV or Parquet loaded and profiled, a prediction contract (target, task, prediction moment, forbidden columns with reasons, identifiers, time, group and text columns, metric) with proposals and proof, the five stages (understand, audit leakage, feature ladder, algorithm screen, tune and confirm once) running on user data through the expansion campaign's primitives, evidence-cited notes per stage, and an export of a runnable scikit-learn notebook and a markdown report. Done when make notebook starts the UI in the ML environment and tests/test_studio.py covers data, contract, engine, exports and the API.

Plan the work and state the decisions with their reasons.
output:
Plan:
1. Trim the Studio: remove the Recipes & traces page (it only repeated the run list), the slogan heading, the three marketing cards, the workspace badge, the decorative pill and the vendor footer; keep the one footer line that matters (research evidence is not production approval); check the data folder file by file.
2. Build the project store on disk: project.json, data/, stages/ and an activity log per project.
3. Load and profile any table, detect the task, and offer the R&D datasets as samples.
4. Write the prediction contract as a typed model, with a heuristic proposal that uses the column auditor of the agent tools.
5. Run the five stages on the person's data with the expansion campaign's primitives (locked holdout, training-only folds, fit-fold recipes, explicit selection rules), so every record has the campaign's shape.
6. Generalize the expansion primitives only where user data needs it: regression without a time column, and two generic feature derivations.
7. Add evidence-cited notes per stage, an optional LLM critique, answers to questions, and the notebook and report export.
8. Expose it all under /api/projects with stage runs queued in the background, build the Projects home and the project workspace, and keep the earlier pages as Library and Lab.
9. Write tests/test_studio.py and run make rd-check before committing.

Decisions:
- The project runs the same deterministic code that produced the R&D evidence, not a new pipeline. Why: Each stage record then has the shape of a campaign result, so the agent can cite like with like and the product inherits the leakage safety the campaigns proved.
- The prediction contract is written and saved before any stage can run. Why: Leakage is the top risk; the contract says what is known at the prediction moment, so forbidden columns are blocked before any score exists.
- The final stage tunes on training folds, keeps tuning only if it beats the default by the declared margin, then scores the sealed holdout once with a bootstrap interval and trivial baselines. Why: The holdout is used once (rule DCLAB-R17); an honest score needs its uncertainty and a baseline to be read.
- The feature ladder picks the simplest recipe within a declared tolerance of the best (0.002 absolute, or 1% relative for regression). Why: A recipe has to earn its place on identical folds; tiny gains within fold noise do not justify extra features.
- Regression without a time column splits with KFold or GroupKFold; two generic derivations (log of numeric columns, pairwise products restricted to safe inputs) serve user data. Why: The expansion campaign only knew a time-series regression and dataset-specific recipes; user tables need a generic default without changing the campaign's behaviour.
- LLM help is optional and advisory; the notebook works with no model configured. Why: Deterministic code owns splits, metrics and selection (rule 5 of the repository); the product must run offline.
- The earlier research pages stay, as Library (map, knowledge) and Lab (campaigns). Why: The owner asked to add the product beside the research, not to remove what works.
